parts.title: The boy who was always late
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Tom was famous at school for being late. If the bell rang at nine, he came in at five past. If a film started at seven, he arrived at ten past, when the best part of the trailers was over. His friends joked that he would be late for his own birthday.

One morning, his teacher, Mr Ellis, gave him a task. "Tom, I want you to write down everything you do between waking up and arriving at school," he said. Tom was surprised, but he agreed.

A week later, he showed his notes to the class. He had discovered that he spent twenty-five minutes looking for his shoes, and fifteen minutes on his phone while eating breakfast. The class laughed. Mr Ellis smiled and said, "Now you know where your time goes."

Tom started to put his shoes by the door each night and to leave his phone in the hall. Within two weeks, he was early for the first time in his life. His friends could not believe it. "I have a new problem," he told them. "Now I have too much time before lessons!"

questions.explanation: They joked that he would be late for his own birthday.

parts.title: How people measured time
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Long ago, people measured time by looking at the sky. [1] When the Sun was high, it was noon, and when it went down, the day was over.

Later, the Egyptians made sundials. [2] The shadow of a stick moved round a circle, and it showed the hours.

But sundials did not work at night or on cloudy days. [3] Water clocks solved this problem, because water ran slowly from one container to another.

Then, in the fourteenth century, mechanical clocks appeared in Europe. [4] They were so large that they were built into church towers.

Today, we can wear a tiny watch on our wrist. [5] Some of them are accurate to less than a second in a million years.
sentences: The most exact ones use atoms to count the seconds.
Many people wear no watch at all.
Everyone in the town could hear the bells and know the time.
The Sun told them when to wake, eat and work.

gaps.explanation: The Sun told them when to wake, eat and work; the next sentence gives noon.
Sundials were simple but clever; the next sentence explains how they worked.
Nobody needed a clock then does not fit; sundials failed at night, so the answer is the water-clock link.
Clocks in church towers could be heard by everyone in the town.
The most exact watches use atoms; the previous sentence says they can be tiny.

parts.title: A note about the timetable
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hello everyone, please read the new timetable carefully. The first lesson [1] at half past eight instead of nine. This means that you [2] arrive at least ten minutes earlier. Lunch will be one hour [3] of forty-five minutes. [4] you are late three times, you will have to stay after school. If you have questions, please [5] to the office. I hope the new times will [6] easier for everybody. Mr Ellis

questions.explanation: The first lesson starts: third person singular present for a timetable.
Must expresses a strong obligation or rule.
One hour instead of forty-five minutes shows a replacement.
If introduces the condition about being late three times.
Please come to the office: imperative form of the verb.
Make things easier is a common phrase; make easier follows will.

parts.title: Being on time
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Being on time is important in many countries. In some places, people say that arriving late is rude. [1] example, in Germany, a meeting that starts at ten really starts at ten. In other countries, people are more relaxed. They might arrive half an hour late [2] still be welcome. When you travel, it is a good idea to find out [3] the customs are. If you are not sure, it is better to arrive a little early [4] too late. Of course, trains and planes never wait for anyone, so you should always leave home [5] plenty of time. A useful tip is to set your clock five minutes fast. It works for many people, even [6] they know it is wrong!

gaps.explanation: For example is a fixed phrase used to introduce an example.
And or but joins the lateness with still being welcome.
Find out what the customs are: question word in an indirect question.
Better to arrive early than too late: comparison with than.
Leave home with plenty of time: fixed phrase with plenty of.
Even though they know it is wrong: contrast.

parts.title: An interview with a watchmaker
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Dell, you repair old watches. What do you love about them?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Every watch is like a tiny machine with hundreds of parts. When I open one, I feel that I am meeting the person who made it.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How did you learn the job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: My uncle taught me. He gave me a broken pocket watch when I was twelve, and it took me a whole summer to fix it.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the hardest part?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The patience. The pieces are smaller than a grain of rice, and one mistake can ruin everything. I often work with a magnifying glass.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you wear a watch yourself?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Always. It is a plain one, but it never loses a minute. I wind it up every morning.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why do people still buy mechanical watches?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: They are beautiful, and they last for a lifetime. A phone will be old in three years, but a good watch can be given to your family.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Have you ever lost time in your own life?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Often! Once I was so busy mending a clock that I forgot my own wedding anniversary.
